cards.headline: Money without a company behind it.
cards.body: A stock is a slice of a business. A crypto asset is different: no company, no employees, no profits. It is an entry on a shared digital ledger that a network of computers agrees to keep.

art.alt: A single coin rests on an open ledger held up by a ring of small figures, an empty pedestal beside them — value kept by the group, not one owner.

cards.headline: A ledger everyone can check.
cards.body: No head office keeps the records. Thousands of computers each hold a copy of every transaction, and they must agree before a new one is added. That shared agreement is what replaces the bank in the middle.

cards.headline: Coins and tokens are not the same.
cards.body: A coin is native to its own blockchain and usually pays that network's fees. A token is built on top of someone else's chain. Thousands of tokens can share one chain the way many apps share one phone.

cards.headline: There is nothing to analyse.
cards.body: Revenue, margins, the price-earnings ratio — every business tool needs a company that earns money. A crypto asset earns nothing. Its price rests on supply, demand and belief, not on profits you can measure.

cards.prompt: Someone asks for a crypto coin's price-earnings ratio. What is the honest answer?

options.label: It has none — there are no earnings
Look it up on the exchange

cards.explanation: A price-earnings ratio divides price by earnings per share. With no company and no earnings, the bottom of that fraction is zero — the ratio does not exist. Crypto has to be judged another way entirely.

cards.headline: Supply is written in code.
cards.body: A company can issue more shares whenever its board votes to. A crypto asset's supply follows rules set in software: some are capped forever, others release new units on a fixed schedule. The rules are public and hard to change.

cards.title: A capped issuance schedule
cards.caption: Many coins slow their own issuance on a fixed timetable: each period adds fewer new units than the last, until a hard cap is reached.

cards.body: Unlike a company that can vote to print more shares, a capped crypto asset can never exceed the supply fixed in its [[1]].
cards.explanation: Supply lives in the protocol's software, not in a boardroom decision. That is why a fixed cap can be trusted: changing it would mean convincing the whole network to run different code.

cards.summary: A crypto asset is a ledger entry with no company behind it, so none of the business-analysis tools apply.
bullets: No company means no revenue, margins or price-earnings ratio to read.
A coin is native to a blockchain; a token is built on top of one.
Supply is set by public code, not by a board vote.

art.alt: A single coin rests on an open ledger held up by a ring of small figures, an empty pedestal beside them — value kept by the group, not one owner.

cards.insight: A stock is a claim on a business. A crypto asset is a claim on nothing but the network's agreement that it exists.

sources.title: Customer Advisory: Use Caution When Buying Digital Coins or Tokens
